title: NRG Security Baseline
status: v1.0 — locked 2026-09-29 after live validation on one tenant (PR #104). Changes to tiers go through docs/TP-SECURITY-BASELINE-CANDIDATES.md first; the test fails if the two differ.
purpose: The controls NRG requires of every managed client, by tier. A desired-state layer over the assessment: it reads findings and never changes them, creates none, and moves no framework score. Assessment-only controls are absent from this file on purpose; absence means not required.
note: Governance only. Nothing tenant-specific lives here: licensing comes from the tenant SKUs (license gating), the EDR from clients.json or -ThirdPartyEDR, skipped collectors from the assessment scope, and approved deviations from Config/baseline-exceptions/<tenant-domain>.psd1.

tiers.Minimum: Expected on every applicable NRG-managed environment; a deviation needs a written explanation.
tiers.Standard: Normal NRG managed-security posture. Includes Minimum.
tiers.Hardened: Elevated-risk or regulated environments. Includes Minimum and Standard.

slaClasses.Immediate: Actively exploited; the day counts live in the operations policy, not here.

freshnessNote: Evidence older than its class window is not evidence: the control resolves NotVerified. Windows carry one day of slack over the nominal cadence so a run that starts a few hours late does not flip every control.
effectivenessNote: Configuration compliance and effectiveness are different questions. EffectivenessCapability says whether the assessment can read the effectiveness evidence today; where it cannot, EffectivenessState is Unknown and is reported as Unknown, never rounded to a pass.

controls.Title: Legacy Authentication Blocked
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Conditional Access policies (Invoke-TPCollectAADCAPolicies)
controls.ExpectedState: A Conditional Access policy blocks legacy authentication for all users on all apps (or Security Defaults is on where no P1 exists).
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Sign-in logs show zero successful legacy-protocol sign-ins over the period.
controls.Reason: Legacy protocols bypass MFA entirely; every credential-spray campaign targets them.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Blocking legacy auth is the single cheapest control that closes the most incidents NRG responds to.
controls.Notes: Security Defaults satisfies it where the tenant has no Entra ID P1. Check for legacy clients (old Outlook, scanners doing SMTP) before enforcing.

controls.Title: MFA Required for All Users
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Conditional Access policies (Invoke-TPCollectAADCAPolicies); Graph: authorization and authentication-method policies, Security Defaults (Invoke-TPCollectAADAuthPolicies)
controls.ExpectedState: An enabled CA policy requires MFA (or an authentication strength) for all users on all cloud apps, and every enabled member has a registered method.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Sign-in logs show interactive sign-ins completing MFA; no MFA-less success outside the break-glass pair.
controls.Reason: Password-only sign-in is the root cause of nearly every BEC case.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: NRG does not manage a tenant where a password alone reaches mail.
controls.Notes: Security Defaults counts only as Partial: registration is prompted, not enforced at every sign-in. Legacy-auth block (AAD-1.1) must come first or MFA is bypassable.

controls.Title: No Guest Accounts in Highly Privileged Roles
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: directory role members (Invoke-TPCollectAADRoles)
controls.ExpectedState: No guest account holds any privileged directory role.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Same as AAD-3.1.
controls.Reason: A guest in a privileged role is administered by someone else's tenant.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: No external identity may hold a privileged role in a tenant NRG manages.

controls.Title: No Application Holds Tenant-Takeover Permissions
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: appRoleAssignedTo on Graph, Exchange and SharePoint (Invoke-TPCollectAADAppPermissions)
controls.ExpectedState: No application holds a tenant-takeover application permission other than documented Microsoft first-party apps.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: App-role assignment delta between runs is empty or explained by a change ticket.
controls.Reason: An application permission with no signed-in user bypasses MFA and Conditional Access entirely.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: App-only tenant-takeover permissions are the modern persistence route and are invisible to the delegated-consent checks.
controls.Notes: Microsoft first-party apps are set aside in the verdict; every other holder must be known and documented.

controls.Title: Conditional Access Policies Deployed
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Conditional Access policies (Invoke-TPCollectAADCAPolicies)
controls.ExpectedState: At least one enabled Conditional Access policy exists and the NRG baseline policy set is deployed (report-only policies do not count).
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Same as AAD-1.2 and AAD-2.3: sign-in logs show the policies applied, not just present.
controls.Reason: With P1 licensed, the CA policy set is the mechanism behind every other identity requirement.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: NRG builds its identity posture on Conditional Access, so an empty policy set means nothing below is enforced.
controls.Notes: Where no P1 license exists, Security Defaults is the accepted substitute and this is license blocked, not failed.

controls.Title: Global Administrator Count 2-8, Cloud-Only
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: directory role members (Invoke-TPCollectAADRoles)
controls.ExpectedState: Two to eight Global Administrators, all cloud-only, including the break-glass pair.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Audit logs show no role-assignment changes outside change tickets.
controls.Reason: Too few GAs is a lockout risk; too many is an attack surface; synced GAs let an on-prem compromise take the tenant.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: A bounded, cloud-only admin set is the first thing NRG checks in any takeover investigation.
controls.Notes: Cloud-only means no on-premises sync on the admin accounts; the break-glass pair counts toward the total.

controls.Title: User Consent to Apps Restricted
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: PIM role policies, consent settings, app-registration settings (Invoke-TPCollectAADIdentityGovernance)
controls.ExpectedState: Users cannot freely consent to applications: user consent is disabled, or limited to low-impact permissions from verified publishers.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: No new user-consented OAuth grants appear in the delegated-consent table since the last run (AAD-12.4 delta).
controls.Reason: Illicit consent grants survive password resets and MFA re-enrollment.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Consent phishing is the persistence route NRG sees most after BEC; users must not be able to grant it.
controls.Notes: The admin consent workflow (AAD-6.3) gives legitimate requests a path so engineers do not loosen this setting. It is a separate control: it is shown here as related context and never decides this verdict.

controls.Title: Break-Glass Accounts Configured
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: PIM role policies, consent settings, app-registration settings (Invoke-TPCollectAADIdentityGovernance)
controls.ExpectedState: At least two cloud-only, CA-excluded emergency accounts exist, documented in the client record.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: A quarterly test sign-in from each account succeeds and is logged (AAD-10.3, manual today).
controls.Reason: Without a documented break-glass pair, a CA misconfiguration or MFA outage locks NRG out of the tenant it manages.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: NRG must always be able to get back in; this protects the client from NRG's own policies.
controls.Notes: Excluded from CA, monitored on sign-in (AAD-10.3 is the manual twin), FIDO2 or long random passwords in the vault. Two or more accounts need a human check that they are the right ones. Partially automated: the tool proves fewer than two break-glass accounts; two or more still needs a human to confirm they are the right accounts.

controls.Title: Spoof Intelligence Enabled
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: Defender for Office 365 and EOP policies in force (Invoke-TPCollectDefender)
controls.ExpectedState: Spoof intelligence is enabled in the in-force anti-phishing policy.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Spoof intelligence insight shows spoofed senders blocked.
controls.Reason: Spoof intelligence is included in EOP and stops internal-domain spoofing.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Included in every plan; no reason for it to be off.

controls.Title: Zero-Hour Auto Purge Enabled
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: organization, transport and authentication configuration (Invoke-TPCollectEXOMailboxConfig)
controls.ExpectedState: Zero-hour auto purge is enabled for phishing, malware and spam.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: ZAP actions appear in the threat protection status report.
controls.Reason: ZAP removes mail already delivered once it is known bad.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Included in EOP; the control that limits the blast radius of a campaign.

controls.Title: Anti-Malware Common Attachments Blocked
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: Defender for Office 365 and EOP policies in force (Invoke-TPCollectDefender)
controls.ExpectedState: The common attachments filter is enabled with the NRG blocked-type list.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Message trace shows blocked attachment types quarantined.
controls.Reason: Blocking executable attachment types is the cheapest malware control there is.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Included in EOP.

controls.Title: SPF Record Published
controls.EvidenceSource: DNS over HTTPS (Cloudflare, Google) with Resolve-DnsName fallback (Invoke-TPCollectDNSEmailRecords)
controls.ExpectedState: Every managed domain publishes exactly one valid SPF record ending in -all or ~all.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: DMARC aggregate reports show SPF pass for the expected senders.
controls.Reason: No SPF means anyone can send as the client.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Domain authentication is NRG's anti-spoofing baseline for every managed domain.

controls.Title: DKIM Records Published
controls.EvidenceSource: DNS over HTTPS (Cloudflare, Google) with Resolve-DnsName fallback (Invoke-TPCollectDNSEmailRecords)
controls.ExpectedState: Both Microsoft DKIM selector CNAMEs resolve for every accepted domain.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Same as EXO-1.4.
controls.Reason: DKIM selectors must be published or EXO-1.4 signing does nothing.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Same as DNS-1.1.
controls.Notes: Checks the customer selector CNAMEs, not the rotating targets.

controls.Title: DMARC Policy at Quarantine or Reject
controls.EvidenceSource: DNS over HTTPS (Cloudflare, Google) with Resolve-DnsName fallback (Invoke-TPCollectDNSEmailRecords)
controls.ExpectedState: Every managed domain publishes DMARC at p=quarantine or p=reject with the NRG reporting address (DMARCian).
controls.EffectivenessCheck: DMARC aggregate reports show aligned senders and no unexplained failure trend.
controls.Reason: p=none reports spoofing and stops none of it.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Enforced DMARC is NRG's target state for every managed domain.
controls.Notes: A documented rollout window at p=none with reporting (DMARCian) is an accepted exception with a review date.

controls.Title: Mailbox Audit Logging Enabled
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: organization, transport and authentication configuration (Invoke-TPCollectEXOMailboxConfig)
controls.ExpectedState: Organization-wide mailbox auditing is enabled and no mailbox is in the audit bypass list.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: A test search returns MailItemsAccessed or similar events for a known mailbox.
controls.Reason: Mailbox auditing is the evidence in every BEC investigation.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: NRG cannot investigate what was not logged.
controls.Notes: On by default since 2019; a false here is deliberate and must be explained.

controls.Title: SMTP Client Authentication Disabled
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: organization, transport and authentication configuration (Invoke-TPCollectEXOMailboxConfig)
controls.ExpectedState: SMTP AUTH is disabled tenant-wide; per-mailbox exceptions are documented (EXO-7.4).
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Message trace shows no SMTP AUTH submissions outside the documented exceptions.
controls.Reason: SMTP AUTH is password-only and is the protocol credential sprays use to send from a compromised mailbox.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: No tenant NRG manages leaves SMTP AUTH on tenant-wide.
controls.Notes: Multifunction printers and line-of-business apps need per-mailbox exceptions (EXO-7.4 lists them) or a relay connector.

controls.Title: External Auto-Forwarding Blocked
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: organization, transport and authentication configuration (Invoke-TPCollectEXOMailboxConfig)
controls.ExpectedState: Outbound spam policy and remote domain block automatic external forwarding.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Message trace shows no auto-forwarded messages leaving the tenant.
controls.Reason: Automatic external forwarding is the BEC exfiltration channel.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Every BEC case NRG has worked involved forwarding; blocking it tenant-wide is non-negotiable.
controls.Notes: Remote-domain block does not stop admin-set mailbox forwarding, which EXO-7.1 catches.

controls.Title: DKIM Signing Enabled for All Domains
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: organization, transport and authentication configuration (Invoke-TPCollectEXOMailboxConfig)
controls.ExpectedState: DKIM signing is enabled for every accepted domain with rotated keys.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: DMARC aggregate reports show DKIM-aligned pass for outbound mail.
controls.Reason: Unsigned mail is trivially spoofable and fails DMARC alignment.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Outbound authentication is NRG's deliverability and anti-spoof baseline.
controls.Notes: Pairs with DNS-1.2; both must be in place.

controls.Title: Modern Authentication Enabled
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: organization, transport and authentication configuration (Invoke-TPCollectEXOMailboxConfig)
controls.ExpectedState: Modern authentication is enabled and basic authentication is off for every protocol.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Sign-in logs show no basic-auth successes.
controls.Reason: Basic authentication to Exchange has no MFA.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Modern auth is a precondition for MFA to mean anything on mail.
controls.Notes: Microsoft has retired basic auth; this should always pass and a failure is a red flag.

controls.Title: Admin Audit Log Enabled
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: organization, transport and authentication configuration (Invoke-TPCollectEXOMailboxConfig)
controls.ExpectedState: Admin audit logging is enabled.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: A test search returns the assessment sign-in itself as an admin audit event.
controls.Reason: Admin audit logging records every configuration change, including an attacker's.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Same as EXO-1.1.
controls.Notes: Read through Get-AdminAuditLogConfig on the Exchange session.

controls.Title: No Mailbox Forwarding to External Addresses
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: mailboxes, inbox rules, connectors, transport rules (Invoke-TPCollectEXOInventory)
controls.ExpectedState: No mailbox forwards to an external address (ForwardingSmtpAddress or ForwardingAddress) without a documented exception.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Message trace shows no forwarded mail to external recipients.
controls.Reason: A forwarding address set by an admin or an attacker with admin bypasses the remote-domain block.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Zero external mailbox forwarding is the standard; every exception is named.
controls.Notes: Named-object check; exceptions documented per mailbox.

controls.Title: No Inbox Rules Forwarding Externally
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: mailboxes, inbox rules, connectors, transport rules (Invoke-TPCollectEXOInventory)
controls.ExpectedState: No inbox rule forwards or redirects to an external recipient.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Same as EXO-7.1; the forwarding-rule alert (EXO-3.3) fires on any new rule.
controls.Reason: Inbox rules that forward externally are the most common BEC persistence artifact.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Same as EXO-7.1.
controls.Notes: Tri-state recipient classification; an unresolved recipient is reported, not assumed internal.

controls.Title: No Transport Rule Redirects Mail Externally
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: mailboxes, inbox rules, connectors, transport rules (Invoke-TPCollectEXOInventory)
controls.ExpectedState: No transport rule redirects or blind-copies mail externally without a documented purpose.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Message trace shows no rule-redirected external mail.
controls.Reason: A transport rule redirecting mail externally is a tenant-wide exfiltration channel and is rarely legitimate.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: No external redirect rules without a documented purpose.

controls.Title: Device Compliance Policies Configured
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Intune compliance policies, enrollment configuration, update rings, devices (Invoke-TPCollectIntuneDeviceCompliance)
controls.ExpectedState: An assigned compliance policy exists per managed platform with a non-compliance action.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Device compliance report shows devices evaluated, not "not evaluated".
controls.Reason: Compliance policies are the definition of a healthy device that everything else gates on.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Every Intune-licensed client gets a compliance policy set; DB-2.1 enrollment feeds it.
controls.Notes: License blocked without Intune, not failed.

controls.Title: BitLocker Encryption Required on Windows
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Intune compliance policies, enrollment configuration, update rings, devices (Invoke-TPCollectIntuneDeviceCompliance)
controls.ExpectedState: An assigned policy requires BitLocker on Windows with recovery keys escrowed to Entra.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Encryption report shows every Windows device encrypted with a key in Entra.
controls.Reason: Unencrypted laptops turn a theft into a breach notification.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Disk encryption is mandatory in the device build standard (DB-2.5).

controls.Title: Antivirus Policy Deployed via Intune
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Intune endpoint-security policies by template (Invoke-TPCollectIntuneEndpointSecurity)
controls.ExpectedState: An assigned antivirus policy configures Defender Antivirus (real-time, cloud protection, PUA).
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Defender for Endpoint shows AV signatures current and real-time protection on per device (DEV-2.x).
controls.Reason: Antivirus policy is the minimum protection for every managed Windows device.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: DB-3.2 in the device standard.
controls.Notes: Where a third-party EDR is declared, this is reported as covered by it, not passed.

controls.Title: Endpoint Detection and Response Policy Deployed
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Intune endpoint-security policies by template (Invoke-TPCollectIntuneEndpointSecurity)
controls.ExpectedState: An assigned EDR policy onboards every managed Windows device to Defender for Endpoint (or the declared third-party EDR is confirmed in its console).
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Every enrolled device appears as onboarded and active in the EDR console (DEV-2.1).
controls.Reason: EDR is the control that turns an infection into an alert instead of a ransomware event.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: DB-3.2; NRG's stack is Defender for Endpoint or Cortex XDR.
controls.Notes: ThirdPartyEDR declares Cortex; the check leaves the score and is verified in the vendor console.

controls.Title: Windows Update Compliance Policy Deployed
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Intune compliance policies, enrollment configuration, update rings, devices (Invoke-TPCollectIntuneDeviceCompliance)
controls.ExpectedState: Assigned update rings enforce a deadline and grace period on every Windows device.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Update compliance report shows devices within the deadline (DEV-4.1); DB-4.7 monitors failures.
controls.Reason: Patch deadlines are the exposure window (DB-4.1).
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Update rings with an enforced deadline on every managed Windows device.
controls.Notes: DB-4.7 and DB-4.8 cover monitoring and verification of the same process.

controls.Title: Unified Audit Log Enabled
controls.EvidenceSource: Security & Compliance PowerShell: audit, retention, DLP, labels, alert policies (Invoke-TPCollectPurview)
controls.ExpectedState: Unified audit log ingestion is enabled.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: A test search of the unified audit log returns recent events.
controls.Reason: The unified audit log is the single searchable record of tenant activity.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Same as EXO-1.1.
controls.Notes: PVW-2.1 (search enabled) reads the same switch and counts once.

controls.Title: SharePoint Legacy Authentication Blocked
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph SharePoint tenant settings; SPO Management Shell when -IncludeSharePointShell (Invoke-TPCollectSharePoint)
controls.ExpectedState: Legacy authentication to SharePoint is blocked.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: No legacy-auth SharePoint sign-ins in sign-in logs.
controls.Reason: Legacy auth to SharePoint bypasses MFA the same way it does for mail.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Same reason as AAD-1.1.

controls.Title: Privileged Accounts Use Dedicated Cloud-Only Accounts
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: directory role members (Invoke-TPCollectAADRoles)
controls.ExpectedState: Every privileged role holder is a dedicated cloud-only admin account, not a daily-use identity.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Admin accounts have no mailbox or license beyond what admin work needs.
controls.Reason: Admins doing daily work on their admin identity expose the role to every phishing email they open.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Separate admin accounts are NRG's own operating practice; clients get the same standard.

controls.Title: Device Code Authentication Flow Blocked
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: authorization and authentication-method policies, Security Defaults (Invoke-TPCollectAADAuthPolicies); Graph: Conditional Access policies (Invoke-TPCollectAADCAPolicies)
controls.ExpectedState: A CA policy blocks the device code flow for all users.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Sign-in logs show device-code sign-ins blocked, not merely challenged.
controls.Reason: Device code phishing relays the MFA prompt; only a block stops it.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Device code flow is an active phishing technique against MSP-managed tenants and has no business use for most clients.
controls.Notes: Blocks some legitimate CLI and TV-app sign-ins; document the exception where a client needs it.

controls.Title: Device Compliance Enforced via CA
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Conditional Access policies (Invoke-TPCollectAADCAPolicies)
controls.ExpectedState: An enabled CA policy requires a compliant device for all users on all cloud apps.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Sign-in logs show sign-ins from non-compliant devices blocked.
controls.Reason: Compliant-device CA is what makes the endpoint baseline (DB-*) actually gate access.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Without it, an enrolled but non-compliant or unknown device reaches company data with a password and MFA alone.
controls.Notes: Requires INT-1.1 compliance policies first. INT-1.2 reads the same setting and counts once (control links).

controls.Title: User App Registration Disabled
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: PIM role policies, consent settings, app-registration settings (Invoke-TPCollectAADIdentityGovernance)
controls.ExpectedState: Users cannot register applications.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: No new user-owned app registrations appear since the last run.
controls.Reason: Users registering their own apps is how consent phishing and shadow SaaS get a foothold.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: NRG-managed tenants route app registration through an admin.
controls.Notes: Developer-heavy clients may need an exception with a named owner.

controls.Title: Safe Attachments Enabled with Block Action
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: Defender for Office 365 and EOP policies in force (Invoke-TPCollectDefender)
controls.ExpectedState: Safe Attachments is enabled with Block action in the in-force policy for all recipients.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Threat Explorer shows detonation verdicts blocking attachments.
controls.Reason: Attachment detonation is the primary malware control in mail.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Same as EXO-1.5.
controls.Notes: License blocked on EOP-only tenants.

controls.Title: Safe Links Enabled and Hardened
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: Defender for Office 365 and EOP policies in force (Invoke-TPCollectDefender)
controls.ExpectedState: Safe Links is enabled with click tracking and no user override in the in-force policy.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: URL click reports show blocked clicks.
controls.Reason: Time-of-click URL protection is the primary phishing control in mail.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Same as EXO-1.5.
controls.Notes: License blocked on EOP-only tenants.

controls.Title: Defender Alert Email Notifications Configured
controls.EvidenceSource: Security & Compliance PowerShell: audit, retention, DLP, labels, alert policies (Invoke-TPCollectPurview)
controls.ExpectedState: Defender alert notifications are sent to the NRG monitoring address.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: A test alert reaches the NRG queue.
controls.Reason: Alerts nobody receives are not alerts.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Defender notifications must reach NRG's queue, not a client mailbox nobody reads.
controls.Notes: Point at the NRG monitoring address, not an individual.

controls.Title: Risky OAuth Application Alerts Configured
controls.EvidenceSource: Security & Compliance PowerShell: audit, retention, DLP, labels, alert policies (Invoke-TPCollectPurview)
controls.ExpectedState: The risky-OAuth-app alert policy is enabled and routed to NRG.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: A consent event produces an alert in the NRG queue.
controls.Reason: Risky OAuth app alerts are the early warning for consent phishing.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Same as DEF-3.4.

controls.Title: Anti-Phishing Impersonation Protection Enabled
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: Defender for Office 365 and EOP policies in force (Invoke-TPCollectDefender)
controls.ExpectedState: Impersonation protection covers priority users and all accepted domains in the in-force anti-phishing policy.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Threat Explorer shows impersonation detections being quarantined.
controls.Reason: Impersonation protection catches the display-name and lookalike-domain phish that gets past DMARC.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Standard for every Defender for Office 365 P1 client (Business Premium includes it).
controls.Notes: License blocked on EOP-only tenants, not failed.

controls.Title: Shared Mailboxes Block Direct Sign-In
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: mailboxes, inbox rules, connectors, transport rules (Invoke-TPCollectEXOInventory)
controls.ExpectedState: Every shared mailbox has sign-in blocked.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: No interactive sign-ins by shared mailbox accounts in sign-in logs.
controls.Reason: A shared mailbox with sign-in enabled is an unmonitored account with no MFA and a known address.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Shared mailboxes exist for delegation, not sign-in.
controls.Notes: EXO-6.2 is the named-list twin.

controls.Title: Alert Policy — Email Forwarding Rules
controls.EvidenceSource: Security & Compliance PowerShell: audit, retention, DLP, labels, alert policies (Invoke-TPCollectPurview)
controls.ExpectedState: The forwarding-rule alert policy is enabled and routed to NRG.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: A test inbox rule produces an alert in the NRG queue.
controls.Reason: The forwarding-rule alert policy is the fastest BEC detection Microsoft offers.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Same as DEF-3.4.

controls.Title: No Allowed Sender Domains Bypassing Anti-Spam Filtering
controls.EvidenceSource: Exchange Online PowerShell: organization, transport and authentication configuration (Invoke-TPCollectEXOMailboxConfig)
controls.ExpectedState: No allowed sender domains in any anti-spam policy.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Spoofed mail from those domains would be filtered; message trace shows no allow-listed bypasses.
controls.Reason: An allowed sender domain bypasses every filter for that domain and is the classic "allow our partner" mistake.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: NRG does not run tenant-wide sender-domain allow lists.

controls.Title: Attack Surface Reduction Rules Enabled
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Intune endpoint-security policies by template (Invoke-TPCollectIntuneEndpointSecurity)
controls.ExpectedState: An assigned ASR policy sets the NRG rule set to Block.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: ASR report shows rules in block mode and detections occurring.
controls.Reason: ASR rules block the Office-macro and script techniques ransomware starts with.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Standard on every Defender for Endpoint client.
controls.Notes: Audit mode first; block mode is the requirement. ASR rules are enforced by Defender Antivirus, which runs beside a third-party EDR, so this control does not depend on INT-2.1; the live validation showed that edge misleading on a Cortex tenant.

controls.Title: Windows LAPS Deployed via Intune
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Intune endpoint-security policies by template (Invoke-TPCollectIntuneEndpointSecurity)
controls.ExpectedState: An assigned Windows LAPS policy backs up the local admin password to Entra and rotates it.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Every Windows device has a current LAPS password in Entra (DEV-4.x).
controls.Reason: Shared local admin passwords are the lateral-movement path on every network.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: LAPS is DB-2.3 in the device standard.

controls.Title: Device OS Version Compliance Enforced
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Intune compliance policies, enrollment configuration, update rings, devices (Invoke-TPCollectIntuneDeviceCompliance)
controls.ExpectedState: Compliance policy requires the NRG minimum OS build per platform.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Device compliance report shows no devices below the minimum.
controls.Reason: An out-of-date OS is a device the compliance policy should be refusing.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Pairs with INT-2.5 so an unpatched device loses access rather than persisting.

controls.Title: Audit Log Retention Minimum 90 Days
controls.EvidenceSource: Security & Compliance PowerShell: audit, retention, DLP, labels, alert policies (Invoke-TPCollectPurview)
controls.ExpectedState: Audit log retention is at least 90 days (180 by default; one year on E5).
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Events older than 90 days are still searchable.
controls.Reason: 90 days is the minimum window in which a compromise is usually discovered.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: NRG's investigation window.
controls.Notes: 180 days is the default today; one year needs E5 (PVW-4.2, Hardened).

controls.Title: External Sharing Restricted
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph SharePoint tenant settings; SPO Management Shell when -IncludeSharePointShell (Invoke-TPCollectSharePoint)
controls.ExpectedState: External sharing is limited to existing or authenticated guests; anyone links are off.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Sharing audit shows no anonymous links created.
controls.Reason: Unrestricted external sharing is how a client's data ends up on the open internet.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: NRG-managed tenants restrict sharing to existing or authenticated guests.
controls.Notes: Anyone links are the specific thing to remove; SPO-1.2 covers the default link type.

controls.Title: Default Sharing Link Not Anonymous
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph SharePoint tenant settings; SPO Management Shell when -IncludeSharePointShell (Invoke-TPCollectSharePoint)
controls.ExpectedState: The default sharing link is not anonymous.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Same as SPO-1.1.
controls.Reason: An anonymous default link makes every share an anonymous share.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Same as SPO-1.1.

controls.Title: Auto-Admit Only Authenticated Organization Users
controls.EvidenceSource: Teams PowerShell: meeting, messaging and federation policies (Invoke-TPCollectTeams)
controls.ExpectedState: Meeting auto-admit is OrganizerOnly or EveryoneInCompanyExcludingGuests.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Meeting audit shows external participants admitted from the lobby, never auto-admitted.
controls.Reason: The lobby is the only thing between an external caller and a meeting.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: NRG-managed tenants keep externals in the lobby until admitted.
controls.Notes: Only OrganizerOnly / EveryoneInCompanyExcludingGuests satisfy it.

controls.Title: Phishing-Resistant MFA Required for Admins
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Conditional Access policies (Invoke-TPCollectAADCAPolicies)
controls.ExpectedState: An enabled CA policy requires a phishing-resistant authentication strength for every privileged role.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Sign-in logs show admin sign-ins using FIDO2 or Windows Hello for Business only.
controls.Reason: Push-based MFA on admin accounts is defeated by MFA fatigue and adversary-in-the-middle kits.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: NRG requires phishing-resistant admin sign-in for regulated and high-value clients.
controls.Notes: Needs authentication strengths (P1) and FIDO2 keys or Windows Hello for Business for every admin.

controls.Title: Sign-in Risk CA Policy
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Conditional Access policies (Invoke-TPCollectAADCAPolicies)
controls.ExpectedState: An enabled CA policy responds to High and Medium sign-in risk.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Identity Protection risk detections show remediation, not just detection.
controls.Reason: Risk-based CA responds to a compromised session before a human sees the alert.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: P2 clients should get automated response; P1 clients cannot and are license blocked.
controls.Notes: Requires Entra ID P2. High + Medium sign-in risk per Microsoft's template.

controls.Title: User Risk CA Policy
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Conditional Access policies (Invoke-TPCollectAADCAPolicies)
controls.ExpectedState: An enabled CA policy requires password change for High user risk.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Risky users are remediated, not dismissed, within the SLA.
controls.Reason: A high-risk user must be forced to change password, not just flagged.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Same as AAD-1.4.
controls.Notes: Requires Entra ID P2.

controls.Title: Sign-in Frequency Session Control Configured
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Conditional Access policies (Invoke-TPCollectAADCAPolicies)
controls.ExpectedState: Sign-in frequency is set to the NRG value for the client tier.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Session durations in sign-in logs do not exceed the configured frequency.
controls.Reason: Long-lived sessions extend the value of a stolen token.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Sign-in frequency for elevated-risk clients.
controls.Notes: User friction; set per client.

controls.Title: Token Protection (Session Binding) Enforced
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Conditional Access policies (Invoke-TPCollectAADCAPolicies)
controls.ExpectedState: Token protection is enforced for Exchange and SharePoint on supported clients.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Sign-in logs show sessions rejected on token replay.
controls.Reason: Token theft is the post-MFA attack; binding sessions to the device defeats replay.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Elevated-risk clients get session binding where their clients support it.
controls.Notes: Windows-only and application-limited today; expect exceptions.

controls.Title: Privileged Access Workstation or Device Scope for Admins
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Conditional Access policies (Invoke-TPCollectAADCAPolicies)
controls.ExpectedState: Privileged roles can sign in only from compliant or privileged-access devices.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Admin sign-ins originate from managed devices only.
controls.Reason: Admin sessions from an unmanaged device are the path from a home PC to a tenant.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Privileged access from managed devices only, for clients that can sustain it.

controls.Title: No Permanent Admin Role Assignments
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: PIM eligibility and assignment schedules, access reviews (Invoke-TPCollectAADPIM); Graph: directory role members (Invoke-TPCollectAADRoles)
controls.ExpectedState: No permanent privileged role assignments beyond the break-glass pair; admins are PIM-eligible.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: PIM activation history shows admins activating roles, not holding them.
controls.Reason: Standing admin rights are the target of every privilege-escalation path.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: PIM eligible-only admin is NRG's target state where P2 exists.
controls.Notes: Requires Entra ID P2. The break-glass pair remains permanent by design. Partially automated: PIM eligibility is read; whether the remaining permanent GAs are the break-glass pair is confirmed by a person.

controls.Title: PIM Requires MFA on Activation
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: PIM role policies, consent settings, app-registration settings (Invoke-TPCollectAADIdentityGovernance)
controls.ExpectedState: Every privileged PIM role requires MFA on activation.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: PIM activation events show MFA satisfied.
controls.Reason: Activation without MFA makes PIM a formality.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Same as AAD-3.2.
controls.Notes: Requires Entra ID P2.

controls.Title: Access Reviews for Privileged Roles
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: PIM eligibility and assignment schedules, access reviews (Invoke-TPCollectAADPIM)
controls.ExpectedState: A recurring access review covers every privileged role.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Reviews complete on schedule with decisions applied, not auto-approved.
controls.Reason: Privileged access that is never reviewed only grows.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Quarterly access reviews are part of NRG's regulated-client offering.
controls.Notes: Requires Entra ID P2 and the AccessReview.Read.All consent.

controls.Title: MTA-STS Policy in Enforce Mode
controls.EvidenceSource: DNS over HTTPS (Cloudflare, Google) with Resolve-DnsName fallback (Invoke-TPCollectDNSEmailRecords)
controls.ExpectedState: MTA-STS is published in enforce mode with a valid policy file.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: TLS-RPT reports show no delivery failures.
controls.Reason: MTA-STS stops downgrade attacks on inbound mail transport.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Regulated clients; operationally quiet once set.

controls.Title: Windows Hello for Business Deployed
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph: Intune compliance policies, enrollment configuration, update rings, devices (Invoke-TPCollectIntuneDeviceCompliance)
controls.ExpectedState: Windows Hello for Business is enabled for enrolled Windows devices.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Sign-in logs show WHfB as the method for user sign-ins.
controls.Reason: Windows Hello for Business is the phishing-resistant credential for users, not just admins.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Elevated-risk clients.
controls.Notes: Hardware and rollout dependent.

controls.Title: DLP Policy Active for Sensitive Data
controls.EvidenceSource: Security & Compliance PowerShell: audit, retention, DLP, labels, alert policies (Invoke-TPCollectPurview)
controls.ExpectedState: A DLP policy in enforce mode covers the client's sensitive information types across Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: DLP reports show matches and blocks, not only test-mode hits.
controls.Reason: DLP is the control for regulated data leaving the tenant.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Regulated clients.
controls.Notes: Needs a sensitive-information-type design first; PVW-3.4 and DEF-4.1/4.2 are the same policy family.

controls.Title: Microsoft Purview Audit (Premium) Enabled
controls.EvidenceSource: Security & Compliance PowerShell: audit, retention, DLP, labels, alert policies (Invoke-TPCollectPurview)
controls.ExpectedState: Audit (Premium) is enabled for E5-licensed users.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: MailItemsAccessed events appear for E5 mailboxes.
controls.Reason: Audit (Premium) adds the MailItemsAccessed events that prove what an attacker read.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: E5 clients get the full investigation record.
controls.Notes: Requires E5 or E5 Compliance.

controls.Title: Audit Log Retention Policy Extends to 1 Year or More
controls.EvidenceSource: Security & Compliance PowerShell: audit, retention, DLP, labels, alert policies (Invoke-TPCollectPurview)
controls.ExpectedState: A retention policy keeps audit records for one year or more.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Events older than 180 days are searchable.
controls.Reason: One-year retention covers the long-dwell compromise.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Same as PVW-4.1.
controls.Notes: Requires E5 or E5 Compliance.

controls.Title: Sensitivity Labels Defined and Published
controls.EvidenceSource: Security & Compliance PowerShell: audit, retention, DLP, labels, alert policies (Invoke-TPCollectPurview)
controls.ExpectedState: Sensitivity labels are defined and published to all users.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Label usage reports show labels being applied.
controls.Reason: Sensitivity labels are the foundation for DLP, Copilot and sharing controls.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Regulated clients.
controls.Notes: PVW-1.4 reads the same state and counts once.

controls.Title: Unmanaged Device Access Restricted
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph SharePoint tenant settings; SPO Management Shell when -IncludeSharePointShell (Invoke-TPCollectSharePoint)
controls.ExpectedState: Unmanaged devices get browser-only, no-download access to SharePoint and OneDrive.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: No file downloads from unmanaged devices in the audit log.
controls.Reason: Unmanaged devices downloading company files defeat every endpoint control.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Same goal as AAD-2.3, applied to SharePoint and OneDrive access.
controls.Notes: Relies on CA (Entra ID P1).

controls.Title: OneDrive Sync Client Restricted to Managed Devices
controls.EvidenceSource: Graph SharePoint tenant settings; SPO Management Shell when -IncludeSharePointShell (Invoke-TPCollectSharePoint)
controls.ExpectedState: OneDrive sync is restricted to devices joined to the tenant domain.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: No sync client sessions from unmanaged devices in the audit log.
controls.Reason: Sync on unmanaged devices copies company data to home PCs.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Elevated-risk clients.

controls.Title: Teams External Domain Federation Restricted to Allowlist
controls.EvidenceSource: Teams PowerShell: meeting, messaging and federation policies (Invoke-TPCollectTeams)
controls.ExpectedState: External federation is restricted to an allowlist of partner domains.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Chat audit shows no messages from unlisted domains.
controls.Reason: Open federation lets any Teams tenant message users directly, the current phishing channel of choice.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Regulated clients run an allowlist.
controls.Notes: Business impact; needs a partner list.

controls.Title: Vulnerability remediation is independently verified against the current vulnerability state
controls.EvidenceSource: Manual: Defender Vulnerability Management console (no collector yet). Device build standard item DB-4.8.
controls.ExpectedState: For every remediated critical or high vulnerability, Defender Vulnerability Management shows an affected-device count of zero, allowing for its documented lag.
controls.EffectivenessCheck: Defender Vulnerability Management affected-device count for the CVE is zero.
controls.Reason: The patching tool is evidence of deployment; only a source that observes the device can say the vulnerability is gone.
controls.WhyMspOwnsThis: Verification before closure is the control that turns a patch ticket into a remediated vulnerability.
controls.Notes: Not a controls.json control and not assessed by the tool: it always resolves NotVerified until a Defender Vulnerability Management collector exists. That is the honest state, not a defect.
